rv.q: Now they've added a third one to the list: 'The Scottsboro Boys,' which opened last night on Broadway.

Of the handful of Kander & Ebb collaborations at various stages of completion when lyricist Fred Ebb died in 2004, this provocative piece appears the likeliest to earn a place among the veteran songwriting team's signature shows

The talent onstage is so lavish it overwhelms our comfortable pieties with pure showmanship, conjuring your applause in waves, then quietly placing an asterisk after each bravura number: Did I just clap for … a shuck-and-jive?
Ultimately, alas, the songs aren't tough or surprising enough to take us beyond contrasts of tragedy and minstrelsy.
In an age when institutional racism endures in more veiled forms, this bold musical keeps you tapping your feet while it socks you with an emotional punch to the gut.
The show's creators have fashioned a work that is at once devastatingly sad and buoyantly entertaining.
The result is a show that is both deeply serious and surprisingly entertaining.
Perhaps with a more nuanced book and flexible frame, Scottsboro would have more punch.

But the music in “The Scottsboro Boys,” with its ragtime-rich score by the estimable team of John Kander and Fred Ebb (who died in 2004), will be softer on the ears of those who prefer the shapely melodies of traditional musical theater to the shriek of today’s electric guitars.
It’s still smashing, and it’s still shocking.
This is the best new musical of the year.
That being said, this jarring mix of racist and anti
'The Scottsboro Boys' sets a high bar for Broadway musicals this season.
Kander and Ebb's score is exceptional.
And while the result is thoughtful, vibrant entertainment, the earnestness and irreverence can seem self-conscious.
But for most of the evening, the adventurous show doesn't fit its parts together very well.
As confounding as this all sounds, what has emerged is an absolute marvel.
This is an important production – though it seems strange to say in the circumstances – a very entertaining one.

cn.t: Critics hail this daring Kander and Ebb musical as brilliant and provocative, using minstrel show conventions to expose racism. While some find the approach uncomfortable or uneven, most praise its audacity, strong score, and heartbreaking power.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
